title: How to Get Members for Your Support Group
summary: How to get members for a support group: validate demand, sharpen your page, promote where trust already is, and turn interest into attendance.
body_markdown:
If you are working out how to get members for a support group, the useful move is to start before the group is built. Most leaders do the opposite. They settle the topic, write the description, decide the price, pick a platform, set a date, and only then go looking for people. By then months have gone into assumptions nobody tested.


Make the group findable early, learn what people respond to, and build around real interest rather than a guess.


## The short version


- Publish a group page before every detail is settled.
- Choose the topic from evidence of demand, not instinct.
- Write the page for one person with one problem.
- Share one direct link through channels that already have trust.
- Make the path from interested to attending as short as you can.


## 1. List the group before it is ready


You do not need a finished curriculum or a launch date to start building interest. A public page gives people somewhere to land while the rest is still being decided.


A MentalHappy[Group Listing](https://community.mentalhappy.com/groups?tab=listing) is free, with no card and no time limit: a searchable page for a group that has not started yet. People who find it can Follow, which costs them nothing, so the bar to raising a hand is low. When the group becomes active, the people following are notified.


**If twenty people follow your listing before you go live, that is twenty people to invite on day one. Not twenty members, following is not joining, but twenty people who already put a hand up for this exact topic.**


An early listing also tells you something you cannot otherwise learn. Nobody follows a topic they are indifferent to. A page that draws interest is a topic and a framing that work. A page that sits at zero for a month is worth knowing about before you build eight weeks of material on top of it.


### You can change almost all of it later


The most common reason leaders wait is that the name is not right yet. List it anyway. The name, the description and the cover image are all editable. The weeks the listing was not up are the only thing you cannot get back.


- Create the listing as soon as the idea is clear enough to explain in a sentence.
- Use a working title rather than waiting for the perfect one.
- Invite people to follow for updates rather than asking them to commit now.
- Look at the response after two to four weeks and sharpen the page.


## 2. Choose a topic people have already asked for


A broad group is hard to promote because almost nobody sees themselves in a vague promise. "Stress support" asks the reader to do the work of deciding whether it applies to them. "Going back to work after burnout" does that work for them.


Before you settle the topic, look for evidence. The questions people already bring you. The theme that keeps coming up. And[Requested Topics](https://community.mentalhappy.com/groups?tab=requested) , the tab listed as Most Requested Groups: support groups people have asked for and that others have upvoted, with the highest-interest ones marked High Demand and a prompt to create that group.


It is an unusual thing to have. A ranked list of people saying what they need, before you have built anything. If you are choosing between three ideas, the one with upvotes behind it is the better bet.


Demand on its own is not enough. The topic also has to fit your experience and the kind of group you are equipped to lead.


## 3. Make the page answer the real question


Someone landing on your group page is not asking whether support groups are worthwhile. They are asking whether this one is for someone like them, and they decide in about four seconds. A blank description and a default image cannot answer that, so they leave and you never learn they were there.


### What a page that converts interest actually contains


- **A specific title.** Name the person, the situation or the transition the group is for.
- **A first sentence that does the work.** Who it is for and what you will work through together.
- **Concrete outcomes.** What people will learn, practice or come to understand. Specific, not thematic.
- **Format and schedule.** How often, how long, when it starts, whether it is ongoing or a fixed run.
- **A plain boundary.** What the group is and is not, including that it is not therapy and not crisis care. The most underrated lines on any group page.
- **A credible bio.** The training, the professional background or the lived experience that makes you the person to hold this room.
- **A real image.** Something that reflects the actual audience and tone. Not a stock sunset.
- **One obvious next step.** Follow, join, apply or ask a question. One, not four.


### Your bio is doing more work than you think


People come to a vetted platform for vetted people, and the bio is where that gets established. Most leaders write three apologetic lines. Say what you have done, who you have worked with, and what you know that is hard to know. It is not bragging. It is a reader deciding whether to trust you with something difficult.


Proofread it. A typo will not sink a good group, but a clean page signals sessions that will start on time.


Every group gets its own landing page at its own address, so your page is not one row in a directory. It is something you can send to a person.[Here is one that does the job](https://community.mentalhappy.com/groups/safe-space-for-abuse-and-violence-survivors) .


**The platform brings reach. The professionalism is yours to bring. If you want help shaping it, the[setup flow](https://community.mentalhappy.com/groups/create) suggests names and topics as you go, and Support is reachable inside the app.**


## 4. Promote where trust already exists


Posting the link once on social media is not a plan. The outreach that works usually starts with people and organizations who already have the trust of the members you want.


### Where to share it


- Your professional network, especially colleagues who regularly meet people they cannot place anywhere.
- Community organizations, non-profits, schools, hospitals, faith communities and advocacy groups already serving this population.
- Your own surfaces: website, newsletter, email signature, professional profile, relevant resource pages.
- Online communities where promotion is allowed and where you already take part properly.
- People you have worked with before, but only where that outreach is ethical and consistent with your professional obligations.


Make the ask easy. *Would you be willing to pass this page to anyone it might suit?* Do not ask a partner organization to explain your group on your behalf. That is the page's job, which is why the page has to be good.


**Check your privacy setting before you promote it. A public group can be found by people browsing the platform. A private or approval-based group gives you more control over who comes in. Both are legitimate. Make it a decision rather than a default.**


## 5. Turn interest into attendance


A full interest list still produces an empty first session if nobody knows what happens next. Every extra step is another place to lose someone, so keep the path from interested to attending short and predictable.


- Say exactly when registration opens and when the first session is.
- Confirm immediately when someone joins or applies.
- Remind people before the first session, with the joining link in the reminder.
- Say what to expect, whether cameras are optional, and whether to bring anything.
- If you approve requests manually, do it quickly. People who wait go cold.


MentalHappy keeps the group page, membership, sessions, updates and payments in one place, which is most of the administrative load gone. You start on the free listing and switch to an active group when you are ready to run live sessions.


Current rates are on the[hosting page](https://www.mentalhappy.com/hosting-groups) . And if cost is the only thing keeping a group from existing, non-profits, universities, colleges, school administrators and advocacy groups can[apply to have a group sponsored](https://www.mentalhappy.com/blog#mhla-sponsorship) so it runs free.


## 6. If it is still not filling, find where it breaks


When a group is not filling up, "promote it harder" is usually the wrong answer, because it treats every failure as the same failure. Find the step where people are actually dropping out.


What you see What it usually means What to change


Almost nobody reaches the page A visibility problem Where you are sharing the link, and who is sharing it for you


People visit but do not follow or join The page is unclear, or the fit is not obvious The title, the first sentence, who you say it is for


People join but do not attend Friction or uncertainty, not interest Schedule, reminders, price, and what you tell them to expect


Then change one thing at a time and watch. A sharper title, a named audience, a different evening or a clearer next step will teach you more than rebuilding the whole group.

## Questions about getting members


### How do I get members for a new support group?


Publish a clear group page early, before every detail is settled, so people can find and follow it while you build. Define exactly who the group is for, share one direct link through networks and organizations that already have those people's trust, and keep the path from interest to attendance short.


### How should I promote a support group?


Start with channels that already hold trust: professional colleagues, community organizations, non-profits, schools, hospitals, advocacy groups, newsletters and online communities you genuinely take part in. Give each contact a page they can forward without having to explain the group themselves.


### Why is nobody joining my support group?


Find where people drop out. Low traffic to the page is a visibility problem. Visits without follows or joins means the page is not saying clearly enough who it is for. Joins without attendance is usually scheduling, reminders, price or not knowing what the first session will be like.


### How long should I wait before launching a group?


Do not wait to publish, only to launch. A listing can go up as soon as the idea is clear enough to explain in a sentence, and the interest it gathers will sharpen the topic, the page, the schedule and the format before session one.


### What if I do not know what my group should be about?


Look at what people have already asked for. Requested Topics shows Most Requested Groups ranked by upvotes, with the highest-interest topics marked High Demand. A topic with demand behind it beats a guess, as long as it also fits your experience.


### Should my support group be free?


Price is one factor among several. Free removes financial friction and can raise no-shows. A fee can support sustainability and commitment and will narrow who can come. Decide from your audience, your costs and your goal. MentalHappy supports free, donation-based, per-session, one-time and monthly.


### Can MentalHappy find members for me?


It can make the group discoverable to people already looking for support, let them follow it before it starts, show you what topics are being requested, and give you a page worth sharing. It does not replace your own promotion. The groups that fill are the ones whose leaders also work their own networks.
